episodes.title: One Extra CSV Can Ruin Your Power Query Combine #Shorts
episodes.source_linked_claims: Microsoft Power Query folder-combine published instructions; original fictional sample data
scenes: Power Query can combine files in a folder, but a hidden backup or unrelated file may be included too.
Microsoft recommends keeping files with the same schema in a dedicated folder, without unrelated extras.
Before combining, look at the file list. Verify that only the intended monthly files are present.
If the source folder has other files, filter the relevant file names or extensions in Power Query before combining.
A repeatable query is only as reliable as the files it reads. Check the folder before every refresh.

episodes.title: Power Query Monthly CSVs Not Combining? Check Headers #Shorts
episodes.source_linked_claims: Microsoft Power Query folder-combine published instructions; original fictional sample data
scenes: Your monthly reports look the same, but July calls a column Sales Value instead of Amount.
Microsoft recommends matching column headers, data types, and numbers of columns when combining folder files.
The column order can differ, because Power Query matches columns by names. Inconsistent names remain a risk.
Standardize headers in the source copies or apply a reviewed transformation before combining.
After refresh, compare the expected months and row counts. Do not assume all files loaded just because the query ran.

episodes.title: Combine Monthly CSV Files in Excel Without Losing Rows | Power Query
episodes.source_linked_claims: Microsoft Power Query folder-combine published instructions; original fictional sample data
scenes: Imagine four fictional CSV files in a folder: January, February, March and a backup. You want three months of sales, not the backup. If you combine blindly, the result may include rows you never intended to analyze.

Power Query can combine multiple files with a consistent schema and make repeatable transformations. Before starting, define which months belong in the final table and what columns each file should provide.

Microsoft's instructions recommend a dedicated folder without unrelated files. Keep only the intended source CSVs there, or prepare to filter the file list to exactly the required set before you combine.

Each file should use consistent header names, data types and column counts. Column order can differ, because Power Query matches columns by column name. A changed header can break the expected schema.

In supported Excel versions, start on Data, then Get Data, From File, From Folder. Select the folder containing your sample monthly files. This is an original demonstration, not a recording of your own Excel installation.

Power Query previews the files. Check every name and extension. If a backup or unrelated report appears, filter it out before loading. Repeating a bad folder selection can create a repeating data error.

Use Combine and Transform Data to open the Power Query Editor. Check which sample file is selected and the delimiter or data-type detection. A different sample can change the steps Power Query creates.

Watch identifier columns: automatic numeric conversion can remove leading zeros. Decide whether a column is an identifier or a mathematical number, then choose the intended type before trusting the combined result.
Power Query records transformation steps. Inspect Changed Type and any filters so they apply correctly to every month. A single wrong assumption can silently propagate into later refreshes.

In this fictional example, each of three source files contains ten records, so you expect thirty before intentional filtering. A mismatched count is a signal to investigate, not proof the data is clean.

Once your query is correct, you can add a compatible new monthly file and refresh. Recheck file inclusion, schema and record counts. Refresh does not replace quality control; it simply re-runs the saved transformations.

Before using the report, compare the combined table with its source files. Verify headers, types, included months, row totals and any exclusions. This small review prevents many expensive spreadsheet mistakes.
